clue.text: Old English player‘s asthma still problematic after taking oxygen

indicators.note: a problematic arrangement of letters is a disordered one
the fodder takes in an extra letter before being mixed

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: An old English sportsman's breathing trouble keeps flaring up even after he is given oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'player' a sportsman; here he is a Tudor church composer and organist. Oxygen joins the fodder before it is mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Tallis was a 16th-century English composer and organist, so an old English player of music.

clue.text: Parts of churches with unusual patterns enthralling son

indicators.note: unusual patterns are patterns rearranged
to enthral is to hold captive

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
s = son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Some churches have side wings decorated with unusual patterns around a figure of a son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthralling' pretends to describe the patterns; it tells the mixed letters to hold S captive.
explanation.definitionFit: Transepts are the arms of a cross-shaped church, running across the nave.

clue.text: Somewhat curious, elegant bird

indicators.note: only some of the words' letters are used

blocks.note: curiOUS ELegant

explanation.surface: A description of a bird as rather odd but graceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' reads as 'rather' in the surface, but it means only some of the letters of the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An ousel (or ouzel) is a blackbird or related thrush, such as the ring ousel.

clue.text: Tree snake primarily eats nuts

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: the asp is a small venomous snake
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: A snake whose diet is mainly nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' reads as 'mostly' in the surface, but it tells you to take initials of both words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar with trembling leaves.

clue.text: Act with elegance on the radio, a way to get into larger venues?

definitions.text: a way to get into larger venues?

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a turn is a performer's act on a variety bill
style = elegance; a stile is a set of steps over a fence

explanation.surface: A performer broadcasting a graceful act, as a stepping stone to bigger venues.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about a performer's career moving up to bigger venues; the answer is the literal gate at a stadium entrance. The question mark flags that playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A turnstile is the revolving gate that admits people one at a time into stadiums and grounds.

clue.text: Someone who sees what you’re saying

definitions.text: Someone who sees what you’re saying

blocks.note: The surface pushes the idiom: someone who follows your meaning, who 'sees' your point.
The setter means sees literally: this person watches the shapes your mouth makes to understand speech.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sees what you're saying' normally means 'understands you'; taken literally, it is someone who watches the words form on your lips.
explanation.definitionFit: A lip-reader understands speech by watching the speaker's mouth.

clue.text: Problem child

blocks.note: A matter under dispute or to be dealt with, as in 'the key point at stake'.
Offspring, in the old legal sense used of wills and inheritance.

explanation.surface: A troublesome child.
explanation.walkthrough: Issue meaning offspring is the old legal sense, as in 'died without issue'.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is a problem to be dealt with, and also a person's children.

clue.text: Terribly exhausted performer dating a real comic character

indicators.note: done terribly means done in a jumble
an exhausted word is emptied, keeping only its outer letters

blocks.note: PERFORMER with its insides emptied out
anagram fodder, 11 letters

explanation.surface: A worn-out entertainer is dating someone; it's a bad idea, and it's with a real person.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Partridge is Steve Coogan's hapless British TV and radio presenter character. 'Exhausted' does not mean tired here: it empties PERFORMER to PR.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Partridge is a fictional comedy character created by Steve Coogan.

clue.text: World leader no longer only wearing diamonds set in genuine gold

indicators.note: a jewel set in a ring sits inside it

blocks.note: just = only
in = wearing, as in 'in a suit'
true = genuine; it takes D inside
D = diamonds, the card suit
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: A former head of state wearing nothing but diamonds set in real gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' does double work: it seems to be a container indicator but simply gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Justin Trudeau was Prime Minister of Canada until 2025, so a world leader no longer.

clue.text: Purveyors of pork pies backing bar succeeded

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word is read right to left

blocks.note: a rail is a bar
s = succeeded, as in family trees

explanation.surface: Sellers of pork pies who are supporting a bar that did well.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork pies is rhyming slang for lies, so purveyors of pork pies tell lies, not sell pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: Liars dispense lies, which rhyming slang calls pork pies.

clue.text: Pair up, as running across sierra together

indicators.note: letters that run about are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
Sierra is S in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Two runners team up as they run across a mountain range together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pair up' looks like the definition, but it is fodder; the definition is 'together' at the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: Pari passu is Latin for 'with equal step': side by side, simultaneously and on equal footing.

clue.text: Catch fish, nursing small chicks

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold in your arms

blocks.note: to net is to catch; it holds S
S = small, as on clothing labels
ling are long-bodied sea fish

explanation.surface: An instruction to catch fish while looking after small chicks.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma splits the surface into two tasks, but all of it is wordplay leading to 'chicks'; 'fish' is a plural here, LINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Nestlings are baby birds too young to leave the nest.

clue.text: Happening the night before and night after vacation

indicators.note: a vacated word is emptied, leaving only its outer letters

blocks.note: an eve is the night before an occasion
NIGHT emptied to its outer letters

explanation.surface: Something that took place on the evening before and the evening after a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacation' looks like a holiday, but it means emptying: NIGHT with its middle vacated.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words mean something that takes place.

clue.text: Before one, people visiting A&E can drink

blocks.note: the letters A and E, which take PPL inside
ppl is the texting abbreviation for people
a tin is a can
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: People turning up at hospital before one in the morning may have been drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital emergency department (Accident and Emergency). Here it simply supplies the letters A and E. The definition is the last word, not 'can'.
explanation.definitionFit: An appletini is an apple-flavoured martini cocktail.

clue.text: Discharge cheers celebrity up if only half-cut

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read the letters bottom to top
each word is cut to half its length

blocks.note: ta is British informal thanks
a big name is a celebrity
first half of IF
first half of ONLY

explanation.surface: A drunk toasts a star, but only if he's half-cut.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-cut is British slang for tipsy, which suits the surface's toast; in the wordplay it halves 'if' and 'only'.
explanation.definitionFit: An emanation is something given off or discharged, like a gas.

clue.text: Where you might drink and dance with child

definitions.text: Where you might drink and dance

blocks.clueFragment: Where you might drink and dance
blocks.note: Literally inside a nightclub.
British slang for pregnant, short for 'in the pudding club'.

explanation.surface: A place to drink and dance, with a child in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the club' is British slang for pregnant, short for 'in the pudding club'.
explanation.definitionFit: You drink and dance in a nightclub, and 'in the club' is slang for pregnant.

clue.text: Travel by boat through outskirts of Dublin in flood

indicators.note: the outskirts are the edges, so the first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of DUBLIN, taking ROW inside
to row is to travel by boat with oars

explanation.surface: Taking a boat through the edges of Dublin when the city floods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outskirts' asks only for the edge letters of Dublin, which surround the rowing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to flood a field or to drown it both mean covering it with water.

clue.text: Continually preoccupied with dreadful bosses the setter has

indicators.note: a dreadful version of a word is a mangled one

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
the setter says 'I've'

explanation.surface: Someone forever brooding over the awful bosses the setter works under.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The setter has' is the setter speaking of himself: I have, contracted to I'VE.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsessive means constantly preoccupied with something.

clue.text: When cycling, criticise car

indicators.note: letters cycle round: the end moves to the front

blocks.note: to slate is to criticise harshly; SLATE with its last two letters cycled round to the front

explanation.surface: Someone who cycles criticises cars.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cyclist griping about cars; cycling here moves TE from the end of SLATE to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tesla is a make of electric car, named after the inventor Nikola Tesla.

clue.text: Speculator tries or he’s bust

indicators.note: 's is 'is', and letters that are bust are broken apart and reassembled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: A financial speculator gives it a go or goes bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a market speculator going bust; the definition means someone who speculates in ideas, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: A theoriser speculates, forming theories.

clue.text: Briefly set up social media site, briefly

indicators.note: cut short, losing the last letter

blocks.note: INSTAL, the British spelling of install, cut short by the opening 'Briefly'

explanation.surface: A quick instruction to open a social media account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' does two jobs: first it shortens INSTAL, then the second one says the answer is an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Insta is the short name for Instagram.

clue.text: In Germany, you formally name a city

blocks.note: Sie is the formal German for 'you'
n = name
as printed

explanation.surface: In Germany, you're asked to name a city in a formal way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to a German city, but the answer is in Italy; Germany only supplies the word SIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Siena is a walled Tuscan city, famous for its Palio horse race.

clue.text: Revealed former editor bored by papers

blocks.note: ex = former
the press = newspapers
ed = editor

explanation.surface: A former newspaper editor exposed as bored by the papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' pretends to mean weary; it means drilled, with the papers inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To express a feeling is to reveal it.

clue.text: Tricky one or a sitter?

blocks.note: A puzzling question or problem.
Someone who sits or poses for a painter or photographer.

explanation.surface: Is this puzzle hard, or an easy catch?
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sitter' tempts as an easy chance; here it is someone who sits for a portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is a difficult question, and also someone who poses for an artist.

clue.text: Relieved, ragged, but not tense

indicators.note: the named letter is left out

blocks.note: TEASED (ragged) with T for tense taken out

explanation.surface: Someone who has calmed down after being mocked, but is no longer tense.
explanation.walkthrough: To rag someone is British for teasing them; 'ragged' here is that verb, not 'tattered'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: pain that has been relieved has been soothed and lessened.

clue.text: Aggressive-looking men caught rebel group

indicators.note: caught by the ear, that is heard

blocks.note: gorillas is slang for big, menacing men

explanation.surface: Hard-looking men detain a band of insurgents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like arrest or the C of cricket scoring, but it signals hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Guerillas are irregular fighters in a rebel force.

clue.text: Antelope from South Africa, India, and Georgia

blocks.note: SA is the abbreviation for South Africa
India is I in the NATO alphabet
GA is the postal code for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: An antelope found across three distant countries.
explanation.walkthrough: The saiga is a Central Asian antelope, not African, despite the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The saiga is a steppe antelope with a bulbous nose.

clue.text: Save reminder to ring graduate about your book

blocks.note: save and bar both mean except
a nudge is a reminder; it rings the next letters
BA = Bachelor of Arts
yr = your, in abbreviated writing

explanation.surface: A reminder to keep phoning a graduate about your own book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' looks like a verb but means except, giving BAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnaby Rudge is a novel by Charles Dickens.
